_about: All book-derived text for The Loop Line. Every "text" and "brief" with "origin": "book" is quoted word for word from the manuscript of The Hidden Conductor (V26). The "_source_note" above each one gives chapter and PDF page (Part 1 = chapters 1-5 file, Part 2 = chapters 6-10 file). "title" fields are short labels written for the game and state no facts. Edit text here; the game code never needs to change.

concepts.title: The scan
concepts.text: The diagnosis was unmistakable: complete cerebellar agenesis. Not shrunken, not malformed — entirely absent.

concepts.title: The question
concepts.text: If an organ this large could be absent without catastrophe, what exactly was it doing when present?

concepts.title: Not equivalence
concepts.text: Her compensation should not be mistaken for equivalence, though the case is sometimes cited as if it showed the cerebellum to be optional.

concepts.title: Unrolled
concepts.text: Its surface area is roughly 1,590 square centimetres in one careful recent measurement — about two and a half sheets of A4 paper, or close to eighty percent of the surface of the entire cerebral cortex, packed into a tenth of the brain’s volume.

concepts.title: Four in every five
concepts.text: The cerebellum holds something like 69 billion neurons — some four in every five you own.

concepts.title: The vermis
concepts.text: Start at the midline, where a ridge called the vermis — from the Latin for “worm” — runs from front to back. It is one of the cerebellum’s older territories, central to posture and balance.

concepts.title: A rough rule
concepts.text: A rough rule: balance, then movement, then thought.

concepts.title: Flat trees
concepts.text: Flat in the literal sense: every branch confined to a single plane, like a fruit tree trained against a wall. Gardeners call that espalier.

concepts.title: What the wounded soldiers showed
concepts.text: During the First World War the British neurologist Gordon Holmes examined soldiers with bullet and shrapnel wounds to the back of the skull — injuries that, by grim accident, produced what no experiment could ethically create: localised cerebellar damage in conscious, articulate people who could describe what had happened to them.

concepts.title: One climbing fibre
concepts.text: The climbing fibre, from a brainstem nucleus now called the inferior olive, was rare and specific: each Purkinje cell received input from exactly one of them. It was a dedicated line, active not constantly but only when something happened.

concepts.title: The numbers on one tree
concepts.text: Against those tens of billions, the cerebellum has about 30 million Purkinje cells, the cells that carry the output of its cortex. That works out at roughly three to four thousand granule cells for every Purkinje cell. Each Purkinje cell receives input from on the order of a hundred thousand parallel fibres, the axons of granule cells, and from exactly one climbing fibre.

concepts.title: Two unequal inputs
concepts.text: The anatomy therefore encodes an asymmetry: massive convergence from the granule cells, dedicated one-to-one connectivity from the inferior olive. One input tells the cerebellum, continuously and in enormous detail, what is happening. The other, arriving rarely, tells it that something went wrong.

concepts.title: How sparse is the code?
concepts.text: The expansion into many patterns stands; whether the code is sparse is open.

concepts.title: A map of errors
concepts.text: That mapping matters, because the inferior olive is not a single alarm bell. It is a map of errors, with different regions specialised for different kinds of mistake: forelimb errors in one, eye movement errors in another, postural errors in a third.

concepts.title: Two kinds of spike
concepts.text: A simple spike is a tap. A complex spike is a tap, then a tremor, then a held breath.

concepts.title: Rare
concepts.text: Complex spikes are rare: roughly one per second at baseline, against the forty to a hundred simple spikes the same cell fires every second.

concepts.title: Not only errors
concepts.text: Since about 2015, several research groups have reported climbing fibres carrying signals that are not errors in any straightforward sense.

concepts.title: What does the complex spike say?
concepts.text: Second: what exactly does the complex spike encode? A binary flag reading you made a mistake is almost certainly too crude.

concepts.title: Which connection to blame
concepts.text: If a parallel fibre fires first and the climbing fibre follows within roughly tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds, that particular parallel fibre synapse is weakened and stays weakened — long-term depression. If the climbing fibre comes first, nothing is weakened. The order is what makes the signal informative: only a connection that was active before the error can plausibly have caused it.

concepts.title: Necessary but not sufficient
concepts.text: This is why LTD is now often described as necessary but not sufficient, and no longer as merely dispensable.

concepts.title: Both directions
concepts.text: That the same synapse can move in both directions was established after the turn of the century: parallel fibre activity without a climbing fibre produces a strengthening that can undo previous weakening, and the direction depends on how much calcium enters the Purkinje cell’s branching receiving tree (its dendrite) — a modest rise strengthens, a large rise weakens, with the climbing fibre as the switch.

concepts.title: The plateau
concepts.text: Smaller errors are smaller violations of prediction, so the climbing fibres fire less often; and as the error signal fades, new LTD slows. The system turns itself down as it gets things right.

concepts.title: Not a clock, exactly
concepts.text: Not a clock, exactly — clocks measure time that has passed. This is a machine for anticipating time that has not yet arrived, and making the body get there punctually.

concepts.title: The conditioned eyeblink
concepts.text: Conditioned eyeblink is the cerebellar version, with one extra demand salivation does not make — not merely that the response happens, but exactly when. A tone is repeatedly paired with a puff of air to the eye, which causes a reflexive blink.

concepts.title: Noise, not bias
concepts.text: The intervals were not systematically too long or too short. They were noisy: scattered around the intended moment like shots clustered loosely around a target without hitting it.

concepts.title: The only way out
concepts.text: Deep inside sit three pairs of neuron clusters: the deep cerebellar nuclei. Almost every signal the cerebellar cortex computes leaves through them, and they are arranged in a row running from the midline outward, in a single memorable sequence.

concepts.title: Fastigial
concepts.text: The innermost pair, the fastigial nuclei, governs posture.

concepts.title: Interposed
concepts.text: The intermediate pair, the interposed nuclei, watches a limb while it is moving — your hand halfway to a coffee cup — and corrects it mid-flight.

concepts.title: Dentate
concepts.text: The outermost pair, the dentate nuclei, largest of the three and most dramatically expanded in the primate lineage, relay signals via the thalamus (the brain’s central relay between subcortical structures and cortex) to the cerebral cortex, including the prefrontal and premotor regions involved in planning.

concepts.title: Brakes
concepts.text: Because Purkinje cells are brakes. Their only output is inhibition, applied to the deep cerebellar nuclei, which are what actually issue the corrective motor commands. A Purkinje cell firing less at millisecond 340 of the vault is a brake released at millisecond 340.

concepts.title: Where the title metaphor breaks
concepts.text: This is where the book’s title metaphor breaks. A conductor stands outside the orchestra, hears the whole of it at once, and tells each section what to do about the others. Nothing inside the cerebellar cortex does that.

concepts.title: Filing a flight plan
concepts.text: When motor cortex issues a command it simultaneously sends a copy — an efference copy, “efference” simply meaning outgoing — to the cerebellum. Think of it as the brain filing a flight plan: before the instructions go down to the body, the same message goes sideways, saying here is what I am about to do; tell me what it will feel like.

concepts.title: The empty glass
concepts.text: When you lift a glass you expect to be full and it turns out to be empty, your hand flies upward: a forward model error, felt as surprise, which is what a prediction error feels like from the inside. You notice the model only when it is wrong.

concepts.title: Why you cannot tickle yourself
concepts.text: The reason you cannot tickle yourself is, in all likelihood, sitting at the back of your skull.

concepts.title: What the tickling result does not show
concepts.text: The imaging shows that the size of the attenuation tracks cerebellar activity; it does not show that the cerebellum is necessary for it.

concepts.title: The loop
concepts.text: Cortex to pons to cerebellum, then through the dentate and the thalamus back to cortex: a loop, running during every waking moment.

concepts.title: Dysmetria of thought
concepts.text: By analogy with motor dysmetria — the overshooting or undershooting of a reach — he named the result “dysmetria of thought,” a term he had been developing since the early 1990s.

concepts.title: The gap between turns
concepts.text: The exchange of turns follows patterns that hold across languages studied in very different cultural contexts: the gap between one person finishing a thought and the next beginning to speak clusters around 200 milliseconds, with considerable individual and cross-language variation.

concepts.title: Not enough time
concepts.text: There is simply not enough time to wait for the previous speaker to finish and only then begin to prepare a reply. The process requires prediction.

concepts.title: Shows up, not yet explains
concepts.text: As the evidence now stands, the cerebellar hypothesis describes a possible contributing factor in some autistic profiles, not an established or universal explanation. The computation shows up here; that it explains what happens here is a further claim, and so far an unsupported one.

concepts.title: A mechanism is not a verdict
concepts.text: A mechanism is not a verdict. Explaining that a cerebellum runs its predictive timing on a different schedule is not the same as saying that schedule is wrong.

concepts.title: The timescale gap
concepts.text: It is the largest open question in the argument this book is making; Part II has to confront it, and Chapter 10 has to add up the answers.

concepts.title: Crossed pairs
concepts.text: Signals into the cerebellum cross the midline; signals out cross back. So each cerebellar hemisphere is paired with the opposite cerebral hemisphere.

concepts.title: Pat and bat
concepts.text: Your lips do the same thing both times: they close, pressure builds, they release. What differs is when, relative to that release, your vocal folds begin to vibrate. In “bat” the voicing starts almost immediately. In “pat” it is withheld — for fifty milliseconds or more, a delay you hear as a small puff of air.

concepts.title: Instrument and score
concepts.text: Dysarthria is a problem with the instrument: the muscles of the lips, tongue, palate and larynx are weak, or stiff, or badly timed, and the sound comes out wrong even though the speaker knows exactly what they meant to say. Aphasia is a problem with the score: the words themselves, or the rules for combining them, have been damaged or lost, classically by damage to the left cerebral hemisphere.

concepts.title: Who owns the clock?
concepts.text: So the cerebellum does not own the rules. Whether it owns the clock they run on is still open.

concepts.title: A fifth faster
concepts.text: And in the morning you are roughly a fifth faster. You did not practise. You slept.

concepts.title: Also contested
concepts.text: The result is also contested. Rickard and colleagues argued that part of the apparent overnight gain in this kind of task reflects fatigue building up during massed practice and the time of day at testing, and that when these are controlled the sleep effect disappears.

concepts.title: Two directions
concepts.text: For slow waves they replicated the downward direction: cortex to cerebellum. But sleep spindles, the brief NREM bursts linked to procedural consolidation, ran the other way. The directional influence during spindles went from the cerebellum to the motor cortex, routed through the thalamus.

concepts.title: Where the fastigial reaches
concepts.text: Where the interposed nucleus projects chiefly towards the red nucleus and motor thalamus, the fastigial sends fibres to additional targets: to the hypothalamus, which governs the stress-hormone response, and to the periaqueductal grey, the brainstem structure that orchestrates the full freeze-or-flee package — the immobility, the blood-pressure surge, the suppression of pain.

concepts.title: Dysmetria of emotion
concepts.text: Until it is, dysmetria of emotion remains a well-motivated hypothesis rather than a finding.

concepts.title: No trace shown yet
concepts.text: No one has yet shown that the day’s learning leaves a trace in the sleeping cerebellum.

concepts.title: A direct line
concepts.text: A single-synapse connection means no intermediate relay stations: one neuron talks directly to the next, with no reinterpretation at intervening stops — a direct line, no phone tree.

concepts.title: The timetable
concepts.text: The difference is the one between knowing a train will come and knowing it arrives at 8:14; the cerebellum would be the timetable. The picture breaks where the timetable would have to span years, which nothing known about the cerebellum suggests it can hold.

concepts.title: Not shown in a person
concepts.text: I know of no study showing, in a person, that this pathway does anything to craving.

concepts.title: Not a moral event
concepts.text: David’s craving at the traffic light was not a moral event. It was a predictive one — circuits firing in anticipation of a reward that his conscious mind had spent fourteen months refusing.

concepts.title: A word that will not stop
concepts.text: Deep inside a gene called ATXN1, three DNA letters — C, A, G — repeat over and over, like a word a machine cannot stop typing. Everybody carries that stutter.

concepts.title: The ratchet
concepts.text: That is a ratchet, and it turns in one direction more often than the other — in SCA1 particularly when the gene passes through a father.

concepts.title: The metronome
concepts.text: A healthy Purkinje cell behaves like a metronome that never stops: roughly forty to a hundred beats a second, every second of a life, awake and asleep, interrupted at intervals by the precisely timed complex spikes that arrive along its climbing fibre.

concepts.title: Before any cell is lost
concepts.text: In SCA1 mouse models, the regularity is disrupted well before any cell death is detectable: firing becomes irregular and erratic. Plausibly, the steady inhibition the cell holds on its targets in the deep cerebellar nuclei weakens with it, though that step is an inference rather than a measurement.

concepts.title: No approved treatment
concepts.text: No disease-modifying treatment has been approved for any of the polyglutamine spinocerebellar ataxias.

concepts.title: Does stimulation do anything?
concepts.text: And there is Patricia’s question, which is also the question that matters most right now: does tDCS do anything? Her trial results are not yet available. The answer, where the field stands, is that we do not know.

concepts.title: Defended, not rebuilt
concepts.text: If what medicine can offer is preservation rather than restoration — if the machine can be defended but not rebuilt — then the question that remains is what is left when it cannot be rebuilt.

concepts.title: The comparator
concepts.text: A motor command splits into the movement itself and an efference copy; the cerebellum turns the copy into a prediction of the expected sensory feedback; a comparator weighs that prediction against the actual feedback. Match -> “I did this” (the sense of agency); mismatch -> “something else did this.”

concepts.title: Agency as precision
concepts.text: On this view, agency is not a faculty one either has or lacks. It is a matter of precision, and precision is what cerebellar damage would take away. That is a hypothesis, not a finding.

concepts.title: Does it shape experience?
concepts.text: The distinction between generating consciousness and shaping it is conceptually clear and empirically underspecified: we have no tools that trace how cerebellar output influences the specific circuits linking thalamus (the relay station between cerebellum and cortex) and cortex that produce particular elements of experience.

concepts.title: When it falters
concepts.text: The book’s conductor has an odd property for a conductor: you notice it only when it falters.

figures.label: FIGURE 1
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 1, Part 1 PDF p. 2. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE 1. The cerebellum in place: a mid-sagittal view with the cerebellum shaded, its three lobes labelled and the vermis marked. The reader should come away with how far back and how low the structure sits, and how much more densely folded it is than the cortex above it.

figures.label: FIGURE 2
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 1, Part 1 PDF p. 12. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE 2. The cerebellar microcircuit, drawn so the reader takes away one thing: the asymmetry of the two inputs. Mossy fibres arrive in bulk at the granule cell layer; parallel fibres carry the expanded signal across a Purkinje cell’s flat dendritic tree at right angles; one climbing fibre wraps that same tree. The visual weight of thousands of crossings against the single climbing fibre is the point.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 2, Part 1 PDF p. 33. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: The forward-model loop. Motor cortex issues a command to the body and, at the same moment, sends an efference copy — the flight plan — sideways to the cerebellum, which predicts the sensory consequences and delivers that prediction to sensory cortex, where it arrives ahead of the slow, real feedback returning from the body. A comparator marks any mismatch as an error, and the error updates the model. This is why a fast movement can be corrected before the body has reported back on it.

figures.label: FIGURE 3.1
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 3, Part 1 PDF p. 39. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE 3.1: The three-part model that has organised cerebellar research since the late 1960s. Mossy fibres from the body and the rest of the brain feed the granule cells, whose parallel fibres run in their millions across the flat fan of a Purkinje cell’s dendrite (its branching, tree-like receiving surface): this is the context, a moment-by-moment description of what the body is doing. The Purkinje cell adjusts the strength of those parallel fibre synapses: this is the decision, and it is where the learning is stored. A single climbing fibre, arriving from the inferior olive in the brainstem and wrapping the same dendrite, fires when something has gone wrong: this is the teacher, and it selects which synapses change. David Marr proposed the first claim in 1969 and James Albus the second in 1971; Masao Ito found the physical mechanism of the third in the early 1980s.

figures.label: FIGURE 3.2
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 3, Part 1 PDF p. 43. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE 3.2: How the cerebellum decides which connection to blame. A Purkinje cell receives two kinds of input: parallel fibres, which report what the body was doing a moment ago, and one climbing fibre from the inferior olive, which fires when something has gone wrong. If a parallel fibre fires first and the climbing fibre follows within roughly tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds, that particular parallel fibre synapse is weakened and stays weakened — long-term depression. If the climbing fibre comes first, nothing is weakened. The order is what makes the signal informative: only a connection that was active before the error can plausibly have caused it.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 4, Part 1 PDF p. 59. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: The cerebellar-prefrontal loop. Outgoing limb: cerebellar cortex -> dentate nucleus -> thalamus -> prefrontal/parietal/temporal association cortex (the dentatethalamo-cortical tract). Return limb: cortex -> pontine nuclei -> mossy fibres -> cerebellar cortex. Drawn as a closed loop, to show that cerebellar “cognition” is participation in a circuit, not a one-way output.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 4, Part 1 PDF p. 60. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: Orientation map of the cerebellum, flattened and viewed from behind, with the midline vermis and the two hemispheres labelled, lobules I–X numbered front to back, and Crus I and Crus II marked. Shaded from a sensorimotor pole (anterior lobe) to an association pole (Crus I/II and posterior vermis). Placed before the first mention of Crus I and II.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 5, Part 1 PDF p. 79. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: Why the right cerebellum serves the left cerebrum. Signals into the cerebellum cross the midline and signals out cross back, so each cerebellar hemisphere is paired with the opposite cerebral hemisphere. Inset: language territories at the back of the cerebellum, movement territories at the front.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 6, Part 2 PDF p. 11. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: The division of labour in a fear memory. Three panels for one conditioned response — hippocampus = context (where it happened), amygdala = association (this cue means danger), cerebellum = timing and bodily expression (when and how hard the heart should race) — drawn as parallel contributors to a single tone-shock memory rather than a sequence.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 6, Part 2 PDF p. 13. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: Fastigial nucleus outputs. The innermost deep cerebellar nucleus projecting outward to the hypothalamus (stress hormones) and the periaqueductal grey (the freeze/flee response), with a dashed, less certain route via the thalamus towards the amygdala — showing the anatomical route by which a timing structure reaches the machinery that expresses fear in the body.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 7, Part 2 PDF p. 20. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: The cerebellar–VTA pathway. Deep cerebellar nuclei sending a direct, singlesynapse excitatory projection into the ventral tegmental area, contacting dopamineproducing neurons among others, which in turn broadcast to the nucleus accumbens, prefrontal cortex, amygdala and hippocampus. Show the return limb as well: VTA dopaminergic fibres to cerebellar cortex, non-dopaminergic fibres to the deep nuclei The novelty to highlight: a structure long filed under “motor” wired into the brain’s reward broadcaster in both directions.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 8, Part 2 PDF p. 39. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: Anticipation across generations. A three-generation family line showing the CAG repeat in ATXN1 lengthening as it passes from parent to child (e.g. 50 -> 53 -> 58), with age of symptom onset sliding earlier as the repeat grows — the “biological ratchet” the text describes, with the caveat that onset age varies considerably even at a fixed length.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 8, Part 2 PDF p. 48. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: SARA progression by subtype. Mean Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA, 0-40) plotted against years since onset for SCA1, SCA2, SCA3 and SCA6 — SCA1 climbing fastest (about 2 points a year), SCA2 and SCA3 about 1.5, SCA6 slowest (about 0.8) — with a shaded band around each line to make the large patient-to-patient variability visible rather than hidden by the averages.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 9, Part 2 PDF p. 58. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: Three ways to silence one bad copy. A schematic of the mutant and healthy ATXN alleles side by side, showing (1) a patient-specific single-nucleotide variant used as a unique handle on the mutant copy; (2) a probe that binds the long CAG repeat more tightly than the short one; and (3) non-specific knockdown that lowers both copies, relying on the normal protein tolerating partial loss.

figures.label: FIGURE (unnumbered)
figures._source_note: Source: Chapter 10, Part 2 PDF p. 75. Verbatim figure brief; no drawn figure exists.
figures.brief: FIGURE: The comparator model of agency. A motor command splits into the movement itself and an efference copy; the cerebellum turns the copy into a prediction of the expected sensory feedback; a comparator weighs that prediction against the actual feedback. Match -> “I did this” (the sense of agency); mismatch -> “something else did this.” The caption can note that cerebellar disease degrades the prediction, blurring the match/mismatch boundary.
